title: TypeScript Fundamentals Part 1
excerpt: Before writing your first Playwright test, you need a basic understanding of TypeScript. In this guide, we'll set up everything from scratch, learn how to run TypeScript files directly, and cover the core concepts every QA Automation Engineer should know.
html:
Getting Started!

If you're learning Playwright, you've probably noticed that most tutorials use TypeScript instead of JavaScript.

That often raises another question.

Do I need to learn TypeScript before Playwright?

The answer is yes, but only the parts you'll actually use.

You don't need to become a TypeScript expert or read hundreds of pages of documentation before writing your first automated test. As a Test Automation Engineer, you'll only use a small portion of the language every day.

In this guide, we'll learn those fundamentals using simple examples that relate to automation wherever possible.

By the end of this article, you'll be comfortable creating and running TypeScript programs and you'll understand the language features that appear in almost every Playwright project.

Why TypeScript Instead of JavaScript?

Playwright supports both JavaScript and TypeScript, but most automation engineers prefer TypeScript.

The biggest advantage is that it helps you catch mistakes before you run your tests.

Let's look at a simple example.

JavaScript

const timeout = "5000";
console.log(timeout + 1000);

Output:

50001000

JavaScript treats "5000" as text, so instead of adding two numbers, it joins them together.

Now let's write the same code in TypeScript.

const timeout: number = 5000;
console.log(timeout + 1000);

Output:

6000

Because we declared timeout as a number, TypeScript understands how it should be used. If we accidentally assign a string, our editor immediately warns us before we even run the program.

This becomes even more valuable when your automation framework grows from a few tests to hundreds.

Some of the biggest benefits of TypeScript are:

  • Better code completion in VS Code

  • Finds mistakes while you write code

  • Easier to understand large projects

  • Makes refactoring much safer

  • Widely used in modern Playwright projects

For these reasons, we'll use TypeScript throughout this series.

Setting Up TypeScript

Before writing any code, let's install everything we need.

Step 1: Install Node.js

TypeScript runs on top of Node.js, so this needs to be installed first.

You can verify that Node.js is installed by opening a terminal and running:

node -v

You should see something similar to:

v24.x.x

Now check npm, which is installed along with Node.js.

npm -v

If both commands return a version number, you're ready to continue.

Step 2: Install TypeScript

Open your terminal and run:

npm install -g typescript

The -g flag installs TypeScript globally, which means you can use it from any project on your computer.

To confirm the installation:

tsc -v

You should see the installed TypeScript version.

Step 3: Install TSX

Although TypeScript normally compiles into JavaScript before running, there's an easier way while you're learning.

We'll use TSX, which allows us to execute TypeScript files directly.

Install it globally.

npm install -g tsx

Verify the installation.

tsx --version

We'll use this command throughout the article.

Step 4: Create Your First Project

Create a new folder.

mkdir typescript-fundamentals

Move into the folder.

cd typescript-fundamentals

Open it in Visual Studio Code.

code .

Your project is now ready.

Writing Your First TypeScript Program

Create a new file named:

app.ts

Now add the following code.

const firstName: string = "John";
const lastName: string = "Doe";
console.log(`Welcome ${firstName} ${lastName}!`);

Run the program.

tsx app.ts

Output:

Welcome John Doe!

Let's understand what's happening.

const creates a variable.

string tells TypeScript that the variable will store text.

console.log() prints information to the terminal.

The ${} syntax inserts variables into a string, making it much easier to create readable messages.

Congratulations! You've just written and executed your first TypeScript program.

Understanding const, let and var

Before learning different data types, it's important to understand how variables are declared.
Modern TypeScript mainly uses const and let.
Although var still exists, it's rarely used in new projects.

Let's look at each one.

const

Use const when the value should never change after it's created.

Imagine we're storing the URL of an application we're testing.

const applicationUrl = "https://example.com";
console.log(`Testing ${applicationUrl}`);

Output:

Testing https://example.com

Since the application URL stays the same throughout the program, const is the perfect choice.

Now let's try changing it.

const applicationUrl = "https://example.com";
applicationUrl = "https://google.com";

TypeScript immediately reports an error because const variables cannot be reassigned.

As a general rule, use const whenever possible. It makes your code safer and easier to understand.

let

Sometimes a value needs to change while the program is running.

For example, we may want to count login attempts.

let loginAttempts = 0;
loginAttempts++;
console.log(`Login Attempts: ${loginAttempts}`);
loginAttempts++;
console.log(`Login Attempts: ${loginAttempts}`);

Output:

Login Attempts: 1Login Attempts: 2

Unlike const, variables created with let can be updated.

You'll commonly use let for:

  • Counters

  • Loops

  • Timers

  • Temporary values

If the value is expected to change, use let.

var

Older JavaScript tutorials often use var.

var username = "John";
console.log(username);

This code still works, but var behaves differently from const and let, especially when it comes to scope.

Because it can lead to confusing bugs, modern TypeScript projects almost always avoid it.

As a beginner, you can follow this simple rule:

  • Use const by default.

  • Use let only when the value needs to change.

  • Avoid var in new projects.

This is the same approach you'll see in most Playwright automation frameworks.

Variables and Data Types

Now that you know how variables are declared, let's look at the different kinds of data they can store.

The three most common data types are:

  • string

  • number

  • boolean

Here's a simple example.

const employeeName: string = "Sarah";
const employeeId: number = 105;
const isAdmin: boolean = true;

console.log(`Employee: ${employeeName}`);
console.log(`Employee ID: ${employeeId}`);
console.log(`Administrator: ${isAdmin}`);

Output:

Employee: SarahEmployee ID: 105Administrator: true

Let's understand each one.

string

A string stores text.

Examples include:

  • Names

  • Email addresses

  • URLs

  • Passwords

  • Browser names

You'll use strings constantly in automation.

number

A number stores numeric values.

Examples include:

  • Timeout values

  • Retry counts

  • Employee IDs

  • Product quantities

Any value that can be used for calculations should be a number.

boolean

A boolean has only two possible values.

truefalse

Booleans are often used to answer simple yes or no questions.

Examples include:

  • Is the user logged in?

  • Is the button enabled?

  • Is the test successful?

  • Is the account active?

You'll see booleans frequently in Playwright assertions.

A Small Challenge

Before moving to Part 1B, try completing these exercises on your own.

Exercise 1

Create a program that stores your name, profession and years of experience, then print them to the terminal.

Exercise 2

Create a variable called failedTests.

Increase its value three times and print the result after each update.

Exercise 3

Create variables for:

  • Browser name

  • Browser version

  • Headless mode (true or false)

Print all three values in a readable format.

Try writing these programs without copying the examples above. The goal isn't to memorize the syntax, but to become comfortable writing it yourself.

Objects

So far, we've stored one value in one variable.

const employeeName = "Sarah";
const employeeId = 105;
const isAdmin = true;

This works, but imagine you need to store information about hundreds of employees. Creating separate variables for every piece of information quickly becomes difficult to manage.

That's where objects help.

An object groups related information together.

Create a file named object-example.ts.

const employee = {
  name: "Sarah",
  employeeId: 105,
  department: "QA",
  isAdmin: true
};

console.log("Employee Information");
console.log("---------------------");
console.log(`Name: ${employee.name}`);
console.log(`Employee ID: ${employee.employeeId}`);
console.log(`Department: ${employee.department}`);
console.log(`Administrator: ${employee.isAdmin}`);

Run the program.

tsx object-example.ts

Output

Employee Information
---------------------
Name: SarahEmployee ID: 105Department: QAAdministrator: true

Let's understand what's happening.

Instead of creating four separate variables, we created one object called employee.

Inside that object, we stored four related values called properties.

We access those properties using dot notation.

employee.name
employee.department
employee.isAdmin

You'll see objects everywhere in Playwright projects.

For example:

  • Test users

  • Product information

  • API request bodies

  • API responses

  • Configuration files

Learning objects well will make the rest of TypeScript much easier.

Arrays

Sometimes you need to store multiple values of the same type.

For example, Playwright supports three browsers.

  • Chromium

  • Firefox

  • WebKit

Instead of creating three separate variables, we can store them in an array.

Create a file named array-example.ts.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

console.log("Supported Browsers");

for (const browser of browsers) {
  console.log(browser);
}

Run it.

tsx array-example.ts

Output

Supported BrowsersChromiumFirefoxWebKit

The array stores all browser names in one place.

The loop goes through the array one item at a time and prints each browser.

Arrays are commonly used for:

  • Test users

  • Product names

  • Search keywords

  • Email addresses

  • Browser lists

  • Test data

You'll use arrays almost every day.

Combining Objects and Arrays

Objects and arrays are often used together.

Let's say a company has multiple employees.

const employees = [
  {
    name: "Sarah",
    department: "QA"
  },
  {
    name: "John",
    department: "Support"
  },
  {
    name: "David",
    department: "Development"
  }
];

for (const employee of employees) {
  console.log(`${employee.name} works in ${employee.department}`);
}

Output

Sarah works in QAJohn works in SupportDavid works in Development

This is exactly how many automation projects store test data.

Template Literals

Earlier we used this syntax.

console.log(`Welcome ${name}`);

This is called a template literal.

It allows us to combine text and variables much more cleanly.

Let's compare it with the older approach.

const browser = "Chromium";
console.log("Running tests on " + browser);

Now using a template literal.

const browser = "Chromium";
console.log(`Running tests on ${browser}`);

Output

Running tests on Chromium

Both examples produce the same result.

However, template literals are easier to read, especially when your messages become longer.

You'll see them used throughout Playwright tests.

Functions

Imagine your program needs to welcome several employees.

Without functions, you might write this.

console.log("Welcome Sarah");
console.log("Welcome John");
console.log("Welcome David");

This works, but it repeats the same logic.

A function lets us reuse code.

Create a file called function-example.ts.

function welcomeEmployee(name: string) {
  console.log(`Welcome ${name}!`);
}

welcomeEmployee("Sarah");
welcomeEmployee("John");
welcomeEmployee("David");

Output

Welcome Sarah!
Welcome John!
Welcome David!

Let's understand the function.

function welcomeEmployee(name: string)

welcomeEmployee is the function name.

name is called a parameter.

Whenever we call the function, we provide a different value.

welcomeEmployee("Sarah");

Now name becomes "Sarah".

The same function works for every employee.

Functions help keep your code organized and reduce duplication.

Returning Values

Some functions don't just print information.

They return a value.

function calculateTotalTests(passed: number, failed: number): number {
  return passed + failed;
}

const total = calculateTotalTests(48, 2);

console.log(`Total Tests: ${total}`);

Output

Total Tests: 50

Here the function calculates a result and returns it.

Later, Playwright helper functions will work in exactly the same way.

Arrow Functions

You'll notice many Playwright examples use arrow functions.

Here's the previous example rewritten.

const welcomeEmployee = (name: string) => {
  console.log(`Welcome ${name}!`);
};

welcomeEmployee("Sarah");

Output

Welcome Sarah!

It does exactly the same thing.

Arrow functions are simply a newer way of writing functions.

You'll see them frequently in Playwright projects, React applications, and modern JavaScript.

Don't worry if they look unusual at first.

After writing a few examples, they'll become natural.

Interfaces

Imagine every employee in your project should always have:

  • Name

  • Department

  • Employee ID

Instead of remembering those properties every time, we can create an interface.

interface Employee {
  name: string;
  department: string;
  employeeId: number;
}

Now let's use it.

interface Employee {
  name: string;
  department: string;
  employeeId: number;
}

const employee: Employee = {
  name: "Sarah",
  department: "QA",
  employeeId: 105
};

console.log(employee);

Output

{
  name: 'Sarah',
  department: 'QA',
  employeeId: 105
}

Think of an interface as a blueprint.

It tells TypeScript exactly what an object should look like.

If you accidentally forget a property, TypeScript immediately shows an error.

For example,

const employee: Employee = {
  name: "Sarah"
};

This produces an error because department and employeeId are missing.

Interfaces become very useful in automation projects.

They're commonly used for:

  • Test users

  • API request bodies

  • API responses

  • Product information

  • Configuration objects

Bringing Everything Together

Let's combine everything we've learned into one small program.

interface Employee {
  name: string;
  department: string;
}

const employees: Employee[] = [
  {
    name: "Sarah",
    department: "QA"
  },
  {
    name: "John",
    department: "Support"
  },
  {
    name: "David",
    department: "Development"
  }
];

const welcomeEmployee = (employee: Employee) => {
  console.log(
    `Welcome ${employee.name} from the ${employee.department} team.`
  );
};

for (const employee of employees) {
  welcomeEmployee(employee);
}

Output

Welcome Sarah from the QA team.
Welcome John from the Support team.
Welcome David from the Development team.

Let's review what happened.

We created:

  • An interface to describe an employee.

  • An array to store multiple employees.

  • A function to welcome each employee.

  • A loop to go through every employee.

  • A template literal to create readable messages.

Even though this is a small program, you've already used many of the building blocks found in real automation frameworks.

Practice Exercises

Try these on your own before moving to Part 2.

Exercise 1

Create an array containing five browser names and print them one by one.

Exercise 2

Create an object for yourself.

Include:

  • Name

  • Job title

  • Years of experience

  • Favorite programming language

Print the information in a readable format.

Exercise 3

Create a function that receives a browser name and prints:

Running tests on Chromium

Try calling the function using three different browser names.

Exercise 4

Create an interface called Browser.

Include:

  • Name

  • Version

  • Headless Mode

Create two browser objects using your interface.

Exercise 5

Create an array of employees.

Write a function that welcomes every employee using a loop.
